events: Napoleon invades Egypt: the first clash with the West
Palestine war and dissolution of the Brotherhood
1967 defeat and the first signs of the Sahwa
Invasion of Kuwait and rise of the Jamiyya
The Sahwa fully crushed, per the sheikh
First signs of the new Sahwa

urwa.by: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh
urwa.s: A secret anti-colonial magazine and network whose secrets are still largely unknown.
urwa.l: The sheikh says al-Urwa al-Wuthqa was a secret magazine. Where it was produced and how it spread its influence are still hidden, and many of its secrets died with its founders. Its influence on resistance to the West is clear, though: it shaped Ibn Badis and al-Bashir al-Ibrahimi in Algeria and Omar al-Mukhtar in Libya. It worked in secret because of the era. Power belonged to the colonisers, and the weak cannot show everything they have.

mb.s: The largest and best-known Islamic group, from which the other groups emerged.
mb.l: Founded by Hassan al-Banna in March 1928, at 22, with six companions. He said: 'We are Muslims and we are brothers, so we are the Muslim Brothers.' Its aims were to preserve people's religion and restore the Caliphate. Under al-Banna it combined tarbiya (spiritual formation), dawah, jihad and politics. It was built on the usra system (cells of at most ten led by a mentor), rising through branches and regions to the Guidance Office. It reached about 40 countries in its founder's lifetime. The sheikh believes it was the Brotherhood that preserved Islam in that era, until the Sahwa. After al-Banna it went through the ordeals of 1948 and 1954 and stayed in prison until 1970. It lost its jihad wing when the Special Apparatus split off. The sheikh holds that from the 1980s it stopped producing cadres: it banned thinkers' books and its talented members left, so it 'lost its historical role'. It reached power in Egypt in 2012, could not run the country, and was crushed at Rabaa in 2013.

nizam.s: The Brotherhood's secret armed wing, created because 'a dawah without power is easy to uproot'.
nizam.l: Al-Banna founded it around 1940 as a secret organisation, because he knew dawah cannot survive without force to protect it, and such bodies were common at the time. It fought the British and fought in the 1948 Palestine war, where Brotherhood fighters were among the fiercest. Then it slipped out of al-Banna's control: members killed Judge al-Khazindar and then Prime Minister al-Nuqrashi without his knowledge. Al-Banna was furious and wrote: 'They are neither brothers nor Muslims.' He is said to have regretted creating it late in life. Nasser was linked to it. Under al-Hudaybi came the biggest split, the Apparatus breaking away, and the Brotherhood lost its jihad dimension.

syriamb.s: The Brotherhood's Syrian branch, which carried the banner while the Egyptian Brotherhood was in prison.
syriamb.l: Mustafa al-Siba'i, influenced by al-Banna, brought the movement to Syria. He merged small circles and scholars into one group and became its 'Muraqib' (the Murshid was in Egypt). The sheikh argues that a group assembled from scattered circles is weaker than one founded from scratch, which is why splits began under al-Siba'i. His successor Issam al-Attar was not accepted by everyone, and Damascus and Aleppo split bitterly. The Ba'ath gradually crushed them, culminating in the Hama massacre of 1982.

jamaat.s: The movement born in the Indian subcontinent; a political party that fought the battle of politics.
jamaat.l: The sheikh calls it the major group born in Pakistan, just as the Brotherhood was born in Egypt. Its founder Mawdudi coined the term 'hakimiyya' (God's sovereignty), yet did not take it to mean staying out of politics. The party entered politics, and he was sentenced to death several times.

tabligh.s: Mentioned as an example of a group that shapes its members in a particular way.
tabligh.l: The sheikh mentions it in passing in the final episode: every group shapes its members in a particular way, just as al-Banna shaped the Brotherhood member. In episode 6 he notes that the 'dawah' he means is not Tablighi dawah. He means dawah that confronts ideas contrary to Islam.

muwahhad.s: An organisation that set out to reform the Brotherhood and saw itself as its true heir.
muwahhad.l: Founded in 1968 to reform the Brotherhood. The sheikh says it has never been written about in detail. It opposed the Brotherhood's international organisation, gathered many defectors and was joined by Dr Abdullah al-Nafisi. It strongly influenced the Brotherhood's international body, until the Brotherhood officially dismantled it in 1988.

sururi.by: Co-founded by Muhammad Surur Zayn al-Abidin
sururi.s: An organisation-and-current that merged Brotherhood activism with the dawah of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab.
sururi.l: The sheikh stresses that Muhammad Surur did not found it, since it existed before him. He took part in founding it and was its most influential figure, so it was named after him, a name he did not want. It is an organisation, with a hierarchy of leadership, and also a current: it moves people and influences scholars and preachers without requiring them to join. Its members brought students from study circles to the scholars' lessons, so attendance grew. To the sheikh, its great merit was combining activism with Islamic scholarship more than the Brotherhood did. Later it leaned more towards tarbiya and scholarship and less towards politics and confrontational dawah.

qutbcur.by: Muhammad Qutb, then Safar al-Hawali and Salman al-Awdah
qutbcur.s: A current committed to confrontational dawah of ideas, neither jihadi nor political.
qutbcur.l: Muhammad Qutb never founded a group, but his teaching at Umm al-Qura University created a strong movement for dawah-based reform. It explained Islam's worldview as the Prophet ﷺ did in Mecca, sought change from the base rather than the top, and refused to enter politics, which he saw as contradicting tawhid. Safar al-Hawali and Salman al-Awdah, the two leading Sahwa figures, carried it after him. Its leaders were imprisoned from 1994 to 1999.

khaliqdawa.n: Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq's dawah (activist Salafism in Kuwait)
khaliqdawa.s: A Salafi dawah that combined preaching with the duty to enter parliament.
khaliqdawa.l: One of the strong movements of the late 1960s. Sheikh Abd al-Rahman dreamed of a single Salafi organisation like the Brotherhood's, so Salafis could have the same influence. It combined dawah and tarbiya and argued that entering parliament was obligatory, to protect as much of Islam as possible. Its relations with the Brotherhood were good at the time.

ahlsunna.s: A group through which Qutb's student tried to avoid the Brotherhood's mistakes.
ahlsunna.l: Abd al-Majid al-Shadhili founded it after his release in 1975; he was among the last prisoners freed. He wanted to avoid the Brotherhood's mistakes, but heavy repression limited its impact. The sheikh says it overlaps with the currents of Muhammad Qutb and Muhammad Surur in ways that would take a long explanation to untangle.

shabiba.s: A Moroccan group crushed before it could take shape.
shabiba.l: Founded by Abd al-Karim Muti' in Morocco. The sheikh says it was crushed before it could take shape; its founder was sentenced to death and emigrated to Mecca, then Kuwait, then London.

shukri.s: A violent reaction to torture in prison, with no lasting influence.
shukri.l: The sheikh says jihadis themselves did not regard it as a serious jihadi organisation. It was a violent reaction to the severe torture its founder suffered in prison, and its influence did not outlast its time.

jihadorg.s: A jihadi organisation from Lower Egypt that later had wide influence.
jihadorg.l: One of two Egyptian jihadi groups that later had wide influence: Islamic Jihad in Lower Egypt and al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya in Upper Egypt. Its members later moved to Afghanistan, where the jihadi current took shape.

gamaa.s: The jihadi group that arose in Upper Egypt.
gamaa.l: It arose in Upper Egypt in the 1970s, and the sheikh mentions it alongside Islamic Jihad. One of its sheikhs, Rifa'i Surur, urged people in 2012 to vote for Hazem Salah Abu Ismail.

sahwa.by: No single founder; a broad current
sahwa.s: The broad Islamic revival that peaked in the 1980s.
sahwa.l: Its first signs came after the 1967 defeat. Most people apply the name to the late 1970s, and the 1980s were its 'golden age'. The sheikh names four providential causes: Nasser's defeat and death, the Juhayman incident of 1400 AH, Khomeini's revolution and its export, and the opening of jihad in Afghanistan in 1979. It spread across the Arab world except Syria and Iraq (because of the Ba'ath) and Tunisia (because of hard-line secularism). Afterwards Salafism split into jihadi, activist, traditional and Jami. The sheikh believes the Sahwa was crushed around 2016–2017 and that a new one is now emerging.

jihadi.by: Took shape in Afghanistan after Abdullah Azzam moved there
jihadi.s: The current that sees jihad as the only path, and later saw bleeding America as the strategy.
jihadi.l: It took shape in Afghanistan after jihad opened there in 1979 with government support, especially once Abdullah Azzam moved there. It holds that reform comes only through jihad, and later that America should be confronted and drained economically until it leaves Muslim lands. The sheikh notes that splinter cells went to extremes of takfir, declaring named scholars unbelievers, and that the jihad scholars themselves condemned them. America struck it hard between 2001 and 2010.

hamas.s: The Brotherhood's jihad exception; everyone agrees on supporting Palestine.
hamas.l: The sheikh says that after leaving prison the Brotherhood's general organisation no longer adopted jihad, with the exception of Hamas, founded by Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. He adds that every current, even those that don't see jihad as the main path, agrees on supporting the mujahideen in Palestine.

jamiyya.by: Muhammad Aman al-Jami and Rabee al-Madkhali
jamiyya.s: The sheikh believes it was manufactured after the Gulf crisis to strike the Sahwa's leaders.
jamiyya.l: According to the sheikh, it emerged after the 1990–91 Gulf crisis and the dispute over seeking American help, and was directed against Sahwa leaders such as Safar al-Hawali, Salman al-Awdah and Nasser al-Omar. In his view its aim is to fight anyone who opposes America, and its arrows target those working for Islam, not Islam's enemies. He cites the proverb 'every thing has a pest of its own kind': to destroy an idea, raise up people from inside it who distort its imams. He adds that not every follower is an agent, since people can be moved knowingly or unknowingly, 'and what counts is the result'. He believes it failed because it had neither a strong idea, nor a strong figurehead, nor a strong following, and notes that it backed Ahmed Shafik in Egypt's 2012 election.

turabi.s: A group that drew in many Brotherhood defectors in Sudan.
turabi.l: The sheikh lists it among the causes of the multiplication of groups once the parent group was absent.

turkpol.s: A current that took politics alone as the path to reform.
turkpol.l: The sheikh puts it in the fourth category: politics only. Erbakan, then Erdoğan's Justice and Development Party, held that political participation and power are essential, while leaving dawah and tarbiya open to others without taking them on. He quotes Erdoğan telling Turkey's Salafis: 'Are you not content that I be your Negus?', and later, 'your Joseph'.

ennahda.s: The sheikh says its positions are barely distinguishable from secularism.
ennahda.l: The sheikh cites it as proof that a group which enters politics wholesale 'dissolves over time'. It reached power months after the Arab Spring, when Ghannouchi had despaired of change in Tunisia.

pjd.s: The Islamist party that reached government in Morocco and signed normalisation.
pjd.l: The sheikh cites it as an example of how entering politics wholesale corrupts: 'the Islamic group in Morocco that reached government is the one that signed and normalised with the Jews; there is no difference between them and the secularists.'

egsalafi.s: The sheikhs who strongly shaped Egypt's Islamic current through satellite channels.
egsalafi.l: Al-Hikma, al-Rahma and al-Nas channels rose, along with Abu Ishaq al-Huwayni (in the sheikh's view the most influential among students of knowledge), Muhammad Hassan and Muhammad Hussein Yaqub. Cairo Salafism included Muhammad Abd al-Maqsud, Fawzi al-Sa'id and Nashat Ahmad; Alexandria Salafism, Muhammad Isma'il al-Muqaddim. The sheikh believes the Salafi sheikhs did not know what to do when the Arab Spring came.

raya.s: The party Hazem Salah Abu Ismail founded after being disqualified.
raya.l: After Sheikh Hazem was disqualified from the 2012 presidential race, he founded 'al-Raya Party' and tried to work through it. The sheikh notes that the Brotherhood pushed him away instead of bringing him close.

ahrar.s: The faction most of the Islamic current supported and directed most aid to.
ahrar.l: The sheikh describes the Syrian revolution as a jihadi revolution that at first controlled over 80% of Syria. Then infighting set in, ISIS appeared and fought the mujahideen, and Ahrar al-Sham's leaders were killed. He sees internal conflict as the reason it never won outright.

isis.s: The sheikh says it 'sadly began by eliminating the mujahideen'.
isis.l: It appeared during the Syrian revolution and fought Ahrar al-Sham, Jabhat al-Nusra and the other factions. The sheikh mentions it as part of the infighting that defeated the revolution.

taliban.s: The sheikh notes that it rules Afghanistan today, after America's withdrawal.
taliban.l: The sheikh says the Taliban, with Arab mujahideen, drove America out of Afghanistan after many years and now rule it, 'for the first time a state free of dependence on America'. He calls it a partial victory and asks: will it win the battle of running a state as it won the battle of fighting?

newsahwa.by: Creators of scholarly and intellectual programmes on social media
newsahwa.s: The new reform current now taking shape through online programmes.
newsahwa.l: The sheikh believes the old groups' historical lifespan has ended and a new current is forming, with new ideas, leaders and goals, 'different, not contradictory'. Hundreds of thousands enrol in its programmes, and most who joined in middle or high school are now at university. He recommends broad programmes for the many (faith, knowledge and awareness), long, demanding programmes for the gifted few, and restoring the centrality of the Qur'an and the Prophet's biography as a guide to reform.

ibntaymiyya.s: Shaykh al-Islam, who understood his historical role and rallied people to fight the Mongols.
ibntaymiyya.l: The sheikh holds him up as the scholar who knew his 'historical role'. He went in person to the ruler in Egypt to urge war against the Mongols and rallied the people, while many Ash'ari scholars of the time fled. His battles with the sects were battles over interpretation, fought while an Islamic state existed. The sheikh says 'his mind lives in his books', which did not spread widely until Muhammad Rashad Salim edited them. He believes the West tries to topple him from outside as the 'sheikh of takfir', or to turn him from inside into a quietist 'Murji'' Ibn Taymiyya.
ibntaymiyya.st: A great imam, cited throughout the series.
ibntaymiyya.cr: Imam of Ahl al-Sunna, reference of Salafism
bk: Reply to al-Bakri
The sheikh takes a rule from it: however careful a man is, some will misunderstand him.

Ibn Taymiyya writes that however carefully a man guards his words, some people will misunderstand them; his duty is to be careful, then be patient. The sheikh applies this to those who blamed Sayyid Qutb for others' misreadings.

ibnqayyim: His student, whom he trained to leave excess luxuries
Ibn al-Qayyim relates that Ibn Taymiyya saw him enjoying something permissible and said: 'This does not befit one who seeks the highest ranks, even if giving it up is not a condition of salvation.'

ibnqayyim.s: Ibn Taymiyya's student, who passed on the discipline of leaving excess luxuries.
ibnqayyim.l: Mentioned in episode 9, describing the core group that carries Islam's banner: they hold themselves to account even over excess in permissible things.
ibnqayyim.cr: One of the imams of Ahl al-Sunna

ibntaymiyya: He learned from him and recorded his advice on leaving excess luxuries.

ibnabdulwahhab.s: 'The renewing imam'; his dawah succeeded because he was a scholar-preacher in the field.
ibnabdulwahhab.l: The sheikh says his dawah was dominant in Arabia, and it succeeded because 'he was a scholar-preacher, not a library scholar or one sitting in the mosque; he was a man of the field'. He quotes a researcher: 'If it is asked, were there no scholars? We say yes, but there were no preachers.' When the Brotherhood came to Arabia, its activism fused with his dawah, so the Sahwa carried his name.
ibnabdulwahhab.cr: Imam of the Najdi Salafi dawah

napoleon.s: Invaded Egypt in 1798, the first clash with the West.
napoleon.l: The sheikh begins the story of the groups with Napoleon's 1798 invasion of Egypt: the first military and material clash with the West, which exposed its huge superiority, followed by cultural invasion, missionaries and colonialism.
napoleon.st: The invader with whom the clash with the West began.

muhammadali.s: Builder of modern Egypt, who sent Rifa'a al-Tahtawi to France.
muhammadali.l: Mentioned after the French campaign: he took over Egypt, modernised it, built modern Egypt and sent Rifa'a al-Tahtawi to France.

tahtawi: Sent him to Paris as part of his modernising missions.

tahtawi.s: Sent to France by Muhammad Ali.
tahtawi.l: Mentioned in passing: after Muhammad Ali took power he sent al-Tahtawi to France, and Islamic names began to emerge amid the struggle with the West.

afghani.s: Advocated armed resistance; 'he never stayed in a country without its people rising against the West'.
afghani.l: One of the leading anti-colonial figures. He advocated resistance and force, and people revolted wherever he stayed. He and his student Muhammad Abduh had their famous dispute when Abduh proposed slow education and he rejected it. The sheikh notes historians are split between praise and blame, and that the era is 'very foggy' and hard to judge in detail.
afghani.st: The sheikh withholds detailed judgment because the era is unclear.
afghani.cr: Not classified by the sheikh; historians disagree
bk: Al-Urwa al-Wuthqa magazine
A secret magazine with a clear impact on resistance to the West.
It influenced Ibn Badis, al-Ibrahimi and Omar al-Mukhtar. Its details remain hidden, and many secrets died with its founders.

abduh: When Abduh suggested taking ten bright youths from Upper Egypt's villages, each to raise ten more, al-Afghani rejected it and they fell out.

abduh.s: Al-Afghani's student, who chose peaceful education over resistance.
abduh.l: He later adopted a method of conciliation and education until the moment came to strike back at the West, proposing to train ten bright youths from Upper Egypt, each training ten more. Historians are split about him. The sheikh notes he called nationalism 'closest to jahiliyya', and that Salman al-Awdah, reading Abduh in prison, was 'somewhat influenced by the rationalist school'.
abduh.st: The sheikh withholds judgment because the era is unclear.
abduh.cr: Head of the 'rationalist school' the sheikh refers to

afghani: His teacher, whose method he later left
He studied under him, then turned to conciliation and education, and they disagreed.
rida: Rashid Rida wrote 'The History of the Master Imam', which records the dispute.

khayrtunisi.s: One of the Muslim figures who rose to face the West.
khayrtunisi.l: The sheikh counts him among the figures who emerged amid the struggle with the West and helped preserve Islam and resist.

kawakibi.s: One of the Muslim figures who rose to face the West.
kawakibi.l: Counted among those who resisted the occupier politically.

mukhtar.s: Libya's mujahid, influenced by al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.
mukhtar.l: Named among those who fought the coloniser militarily, and among those shaped by al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.

ibnbadis.s: Pioneer of reform in Algeria, author of the famous fatwa on naturalisation.
ibnbadis.l: One of the figures who resisted colonialism in Algeria and was influenced by al-Urwa al-Wuthqa. He addressed nationalism and naturalisation and issued his famous fatwa, which al-Tahir Ibn Ashur answered.
ibnbadis.st: A figure of resistance and reform.

ibrahimi: His companion in reform in Algeria
The sheikh names them together as Algeria's figures of resistance.

ibrahimi.s: A figure of resistance in Algeria, influenced by al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.
ibrahimi.l: Named with Ibn Badis among those who resisted the coloniser and were influenced by al-Urwa al-Wuthqa.

ibnbadis: Worked with him in reform in Algeria.

khattabi.s: Leader of the resistance in Morocco's Rif.
khattabi.l: Named among those who resisted the coloniser in Morocco.

ibnashur.s: Tunisia's scholar, who answered Ibn Badis on naturalisation.
ibnashur.l: Mentioned in the debate over nationalism and naturalisation: Ibn Badis issued his famous fatwa and Ibn Ashur replied.

ibnbadis: Replied to Ibn Badis's famous fatwa on naturalisation.

rida.s: Hassan al-Banna's teacher, who wrote on the Caliphate after its fall.
rida.l: When the Caliphate fell he wrote on 'The Caliphate or the Supreme Imamate'. Reform leaders then hoped to move the Caliphate to Egypt. He was Hassan al-Banna's teacher, and wrote Muhammad Abduh's biography in 'The History of the Master Imam'.
rida.st: Mentioned with respect as al-Banna's teacher.
bk: The Caliphate or the Supreme Imamate
Written when the Caliphate fell, to preserve the idea of the state in Islam.
Written when reformers feared people would grow up outside Islam under man-made laws taken from France and Britain.
The History of the Master Imam
Records the famous dispute between al-Afghani and Abduh.
The sheikh's source for Abduh's proposal to train ten bright youths and al-Afghani's rejection.

banna: Al-Banna studied under Rida and inherited his concern to restore the Caliphate.
abduh: The teacher whose biography he wrote
Wrote his life in The History of the Master Imam.

qasimamin.s: One of the nominal Muslims who began attacking the foundations of Islam.
qasimamin.l: The sheikh says the battles over Islam's foundations began before the Caliphate fell, waged by people counted as Muslims rather than by the West, among them Qasim Amin in his two books.
bk: The Liberation of Women
One of the books that came out one after another to topple Islam's foundations.
The sheikh sees it as the first link in the internal campaign against Islam's foundations.
The New Woman
The second book in the same vein.
Mentioned with The Liberation of Women.

abdulraziq.s: Wrote 'Islam and the Foundations of Governance' to deny that Islam brought a state.
abdulraziq.l: After the Caliphate fell he wrote his book to topple the Islamic idea that Islam came with a state.
abdulraziq.st: Attacked the principle of the state in Islam.
bk: Islam and the Foundations of Governance
Aimed to deny that Islam is religion and state.
The sheikh replies that Islam is a religion that contains its state, and its laws can only be applied by a state that rules by it.

tahahussein.s: Attacked the Qur'an in 'On Pre-Islamic Poetry'.
tahahussein.l: He wrote 'On Pre-Islamic Poetry' to undermine the Qur'an. Al-Rafi'i and his student Mahmoud Shakir answered him. The sheikh believes most of the last century's books on the Qur'an's inimitability were written in response to this war.
tahahussein.st: Head of a school opposed to the defence of Islam.
bk: On Pre-Islamic Poetry
A book attacking the Qur'an.
It started a great literary battle: al-Rafi'i answered it in 'Under the Banner of the Qur'an' and Mahmoud Shakir fought it too.

rafii.s: Answered Taha Hussein in 'Under the Banner of the Qur'an'.
rafii.l: He and his student Mahmoud Shakir fought the 'battle of the men of letters' in defence of Islam, answering Taha Hussein.
rafii.st: A defender of the Qur'an in the literary battle.
bk: Under the Banner of the Qur'an
A reply to 'On Pre-Islamic Poetry'.
It opened the way for the books defending the Qur'an that followed.

mahmoudshakir: Carried the defence of Islam in literature with him.

mahmoudshakir.s: Al-Rafi'i's student, who defended Islam in literature.
mahmoudshakir.l: Mentioned with his teacher al-Rafi'i, confronting Taha Hussein's school.
mahmoudshakir.st: A defender of Islam in literature.

aqqad.s: Head of the 'third school' in the battle of the men of letters.
aqqad.l: Passing mention: there was al-Rafi'i's school, Taha Hussein's, and a third, al-Aqqad's.

ataturk.l: The sheikh notes al-Banna was about 17 when Atatürk abolished the Caliphate, after which states became independent and ruled by man-made laws, to the point of licensing brothels and bars.

banna.s: Founder of the Muslim Brotherhood, 'the most prominent name in modern Islamic history'.
banna.l: The sheikh describes him as rarely gifted: charismatic, calm, knowing more than ten thousand lines of poetry by heart. As a youth he went to the Sheikh of al-Azhar in tears, asking him to defend Islam. He founded the group in 1928 and built it from 1928 to 1939. He preached in more than twenty cafés a night, in talks of five to ten minutes, dressed like ordinary people. He wrote a book of fiqh on the four schools, then burned it, judging field work more powerful than books. A million people once marched with him, when Egypt had fewer than twenty million. He was assassinated in February 1949, aged 43. The sheikh counts as his genius the idea of detaching twenty of the brightest Brothers to do politics, protecting the dawah without the group bearing the cost of their statements: 'To this day there is no better ijtihad.'
banna.st: A genius of dawah and organisation; his mistakes were good-faith judgments.
bk: Memoirs of the Dawah and the Preacher
Tells of the seventy-year-old sheikh who insisted al-Banna lead.
The sheikh cites the elderly scholar who heard al-Banna's dawah, joined him and wanted to put him forward as leader; al-Banna refused, knowing only he was suited to it.
A fiqh book on the four schools (burned)
Burned so it would not become a source of prestige.
He felt his duty at that stage was the battle of dawah in the field, which he judged far more powerful than books.

rida: Learned from Rashid Rida and carried his concern to restore the Caliphate.
nuqrashi: Al-Nuqrashi dissolved the group on 8 December 1948 and jailed its members.
faridabdulkhaliq: Paid his own train fare, telling him 'you give to the dawah, you don't take from it', and handed him an article to publish on his engagement day.

faridabdulkhaliq.s: Al-Banna's close student, witness to his character on 'Witness to the Era'.
faridabdulkhaliq.l: He related that he saw al-Banna angry only once, when Special Apparatus members disobeyed him and killed Judge al-Khazindar; al-Banna pulled at his hair, saying 'I build and they destroy.' He also told how al-Banna paid his own train fare to teach him giving.
faridabdulkhaliq.st: A reliable source on al-Banna's life.

banna: Told many stories of him on Witness to the Era.

nuqrashi.s: Dissolved the Muslim Brotherhood on 8 December 1948.
nuqrashi.l: He dissolved the group and jailed its members; Special Apparatus members killed him, and al-Banna, furious, wrote 'they are neither brothers nor Muslims'.

banna: Dissolved the group and imprisoned its members.

hudaybi.s: The judge who succeeded al-Banna as Murshid but could not fill his place.
hudaybi.l: A judge who left the bench to become Murshid, about 15 years older than al-Banna. The sheikh gives two reasons he could not replace him: al-Banna was the founder, and followers are most influenced by their first teacher; and al-Hudaybi lacked al-Banna's abilities. He tried to bring the Special Apparatus back under control, and accepted the coup against the monarchy on condition the Free Officers bore responsibility for it. Later some Brothers accepted 'half-solutions' with Nasser. The biggest splits happened under him, and the book 'Preachers, Not Judges' is attributed to him, though it is said Egyptian security wrote it.
bk: Preachers, Not Judges
The first attack on Sayyid Qutb from inside the Brotherhood; said to have been written by Egyptian security.
The Brotherhood disagreed whether it answered 'Milestones' or those who misread Qutb. After it, the Brotherhood gave up the option of jihad.

qutb: Credited with the reply to Milestones
Preachers, Not Judges is said to answer Qutb, or those who misread him.
nasser: Negotiated with him, then Nasser turned on him
Nasser sat with him, some Brothers accepted half-solutions, then he crushed them.

nasser.s: 'The trial of the world'; turned on the Brotherhood and executed Sayyid Qutb.
nasser.l: He was with the Special Apparatus and the Free Officers, then deputy to Muhammad Naguib. He tried and failed to win over the Brotherhood, then overthrew Naguib in 1954 and turned on the Brotherhood, jailing them. He seduced people from their religion: they named their sons after him and wept when he died in 1970. He refused to spare Sayyid Qutb, and ordered that Ibn Baz's letter of intercession stay sealed until the execution was carried out. He was defeated in 1967, and Nasserism fell with him.

qutb: Sentenced him to death and carried it out in 1966.
hudaybi: Turned on the Brotherhood after the negotiations.

naguib.s: The first ruler after the July Revolution, overthrown by Nasser.
naguib.l: Made ruler after the revolution with Nasser as his deputy, then Nasser took power from him.

qutb.s: 'The most dangerous man to the West in the last century'; moved the Islamic current from defence to attack.
qutb.l: In America he heard church bells celebrating al-Banna's killing, and it struck him. Later the Interior Minister asked whether he was with the Brotherhood, and he replied, 'Consider me with the Brotherhood from this moment', so he joined and filled a great vacuum. He spent about ten years in prison from 1954, writing his most important books there, and was executed in 1966 after the 1965 organisation case. He said: 'Killing Nasser is a trivial goal; we aim to build a nation that does not produce a Nasser.' The sheikh believes every later current, activist, scholarly and jihadi alike, was built on his literature of pride in faith. He names three merits: highlighting the activist method of dawah, instilling pride through faith, and the artistic imagery of the Qur'an. He wrote in a literary style rather than legal rulings, so he told his student al-Shadhili to turn it into fiqh.
qutb.st: Central; his books are still essential because they hold 'the author's mind'.
qutb.cr: Broadly Salafi in creed, opposed the theologians, with errors like those of al-Qurtubi and Ibn Hajar
bk: In the Shade of the Qur'an
Written in prison with Ibn Kathir's tafsir at hand, rewritten three times.

He finished the new method for the first ten parts and the last three. His books were shown to Muhammad al-Ghazali, who approved them except for Surat al-Buruj. In the 1980s it was read in mosques and even on some radio stations.
Milestones
Opens with 'a unique Qur'anic generation'; 'Preachers, Not Judges' is said to answer it.

In it he answers Malik Bennabi on the concept of civilisation. Raed Salah relates that Hebrew University lecturers grew angry when a student mentioned it. Al-Albani said some of its words 'have light'.
This Religion
Written for the shock on the Brothers' faces when they entered prison.
They had expected to reach power and found themselves in prison, so he explained the nature of this religion and that trials are inevitable. A small book of great benefit.
The Future Belongs to This Religion
Certainty that the future is Islam's, with the outcome in God's hands.
Speaks of the reserve of human nature, experience and trial, and of an easy, effective method.
Artistic Imagery in the Qur'an
Opened the study of the Qur'an's beauty, which 'did not exist before him'.
With 'Scenes of the Resurrection in the Qur'an' and 'Characteristics of the Islamic Worldview', one of the doors the sheikh says God opened for him.
The poem 'Hubal'
A reply to Nasser.
Mentioned in the context of the clash with Nasser before the second ordeal.

banna: Wrote 'Hassan al-Banna and the genius of building': his name means 'the builder' and he built the Brotherhood well.
nasser: Refused to sign an apology: 'This index finger that testifies to God's oneness refuses to sign for a tyrant.'
muhammadqutb: His brother, who carried his legacy
Muhammad Qutb mined Sayyid's legacy and developed it.
shadhili: Told him to turn his literary books into legal rulings.
ghazali: Al-Ghazali approved his books except the part on Surat al-Buruj.
bennabi: Replied to Malik Bennabi in Milestones.

muhammadqutb.s: Carried his brother's legacy and founded the dawah reform current from Umm al-Qura University.
muhammadqutb.l: After prison he went to Mecca, taught at Umm al-Qura University, headed the Department of Creed and Dawah, and founded the subject 'Contemporary Intellectual Doctrines'. The sheikh calls him 'the only man who fought Islam's battle on every front', writing on everything. He rejected politics until his death in 2014 at 95, seeing it as contrary to tawhid. He left the Brotherhood organisationally without announcing a split. In 'How Do We Call People' he faulted al-Banna for expanding before building a solid base; the sheikh finds this 'true as a statement but not accurate in application'. Asked about his brother, he said: 'Ask Salah Abd al-Fattah; he knows Sayyid better than I do.'
muhammadqutb.st: One of the greatest writers in Islam's battles.
muhammadqutb.cr: Not explicitly classified by the sheikh
bk: How Do We Call People
Faults al-Banna for expanding before building a solid base.
He held that a solid, thoroughly trained core must exist before mass expansion. The sheikh replies that the core did exist, and the masses reached leadership only in the Special Apparatus.
Our Contemporary Reality
Greatly influenced the Brotherhood.
One of the books he wrote to guide the Brotherhood, and highly influential.
Contemporary Intellectual Doctrines
Founded a course at Umm al-Qura with it.
A tool in his battle with secularism and modern ideologies; Safar al-Hawali's thesis on secularism came from it.

safar: The student who carried his banner
Safar adopted his view of change from the base.
banna: Criticised his expansion before a solid base
Deeply respected him but saw haste as his mistake.
salahkhalidi: Referred people to him on his brother's life
Said: he knows Sayyid better than I do.

shadhili.s: Sayyid Qutb's close student, who turned his books into legal rulings.
shadhili.l: Imprisoned with Qutb in 1965 and among the last released, in 1975. He decided to found a new group that would avoid the Brotherhood's mistakes.
bk: The Boundary of Islam and the Reality of Faith
Turned Qutb's literary books into legal rulings at his request.
Because Qutb wrote in a literary style, it is a mistake to take legal rulings from him directly.

qutb: Imprisoned with him; turned his books into fiqh.
hudaybi: One of the strong reactions to 'Preachers, Not Judges'
The sheikh counts him among influential figures in the Brotherhood who pushed back against that trend.

ghazali.s: Split from the Brotherhood under al-Hudaybi; held mistaken views that Ibn Baz gently advised him on.
ghazali.l: One of the influential thinkers who split from the Brotherhood. Qutb's books were shown to him and he approved them. He wrote 'Fiqh al-Sira', influenced by Qutb's activist method. The sheikh says he held 'mistaken views far from the truth', and Ibn Baz advised him kindly. Salman al-Awdah answered him in 'A Calm Dialogue with Muhammad al-Ghazali'.
ghazali.st: Has merit, but held mistaken views.
bk: Fiqh al-Sira
One of the books influenced by the activist method Qutb highlighted.
The sheikh counts it among biographies of the Prophet shaped by Qutb.

qutb: Approved them except the part on Surat al-Buruj.

sayyidsabiq.s: One of the leaders who split from the Brotherhood under al-Hudaybi.
sayyidsabiq.l: Mentioned with Muhammad al-Ghazali among the biggest splits in the Brotherhood's history.

sibai.s: 'One of the greatest men'; brought the Brotherhood to Syria and carried the banner after the Egyptians were jailed.
sibai.l: He met al-Banna and was influenced by him: intelligent, strong, an eloquent orator. He gathered scholars and committed youth into the Syrian branch and became its Muraqib, fighting on political and dawah fronts and answering the Orientalists. He lost an election to an alliance of Ba'athists, nationalists and communists, joined by a Sufi sheikh; his illness worsened into paralysis, and the sheikh says he went to Lebanon and died there.

banna: Met al-Banna and brought his dawah to Syria.
kuftaro: The Sufi sheikh sided with his rivals.
issamattar: Took up the banner after him.

issamattar.s: Al-Siba'i's successor in Damascus, not accepted by all the Syrian Brothers.
issamattar.l: Under him a bitter split opened between the Damascus and Aleppo Brothers; he believed he was most entitled to lead, and the Syrian Brotherhood fell apart. Muhammad Surur was his student. The sheikh mentioned him as alive and nearly a hundred (he said in Britain; he is generally known to have lived in Aachen, Germany).
issamattar.st: The Brotherhood did not unite behind him.

surur: Muhammad Surur studied under him, then left the Brotherhood.

kuftaro.s: The Sufi sheikh who stood against al-Siba'i in the election.
kuftaro.l: The sheikh reports he said: 'I saw al-Maliki in a car with the Prophet ﷺ riding with us; this nation only moves with al-Maliki', and this al-Maliki was reportedly an atheist. When scholars advised him he would say: 'Tomorrow is near for whoever waits.'
kuftaro.st: Sided with the secularists against the Islamists.

sibai: Joined Ba'athists, nationalists and communists against the Islamists.

surur.s: An open Salafi who merged Brotherhood activism with Islamic scholarship; the Sururi current bears his name.
surur.l: A student of Issam al-Attar, he split from the Syrian Brotherhood and moved to Saudi Arabia (Ha'il, then Qassim, then al-Ahsa), then Kuwait for 11 years, then London and Jordan, and died in Qatar. He was Salafi before reaching Arabia and openly so, yet called for unity: 'Why not unite with the Brotherhood on the 70% we agree on and differ on the 30%?' He wrote books refuting the jihadis, and 'Then Came the Turn of the Magians' under a pseudonym. With the Sahwa scholars he rejected seeking non-Muslim help in the Gulf crisis.
surur.st: His merit is combining activism with scholarship.
bk: Ruling by Other Than What God Revealed, and the Extremists
One of his books refuting the jihadis.
Written in the 1990s, when the conflict between the dawah and jihadi currents intensified.
Then Came the Turn of the Magians
Written under the pseudonym 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad', warning of the Shi'a expansion.
Reflects the Sahwa's focus on answering the Shi'a after the Iranian revolution.

salman: Salman al-Awdah studied under him in the second year of middle school.
banna: Called for unity with the Brotherhood
Wanted to unite on common ground, but the Brotherhood attacked him.

mamun.s: Founder of the Unified Organization to reform the Brotherhood.
mamun.l: Not well known, says the sheikh, but his organisation drew many Brotherhood defectors and influenced its international body. The sheikh said he died 'last year'.

nafisi.s: 'One of the best-known thinkers to leave the Brotherhood', whose books it banned.
nafisi.l: He joined the Unified Organization. In the 1980s the Brotherhood banned thinkers' books, including al-Nafisi's, which the sheikh sees as a sign it had lost its historical role.

abdulkhaliq.s: 'A renewer for Salafis in the political field'; held that entering parliament is obligatory.
abdulkhaliq.l: As a child his father took him to al-Banna, who prayed for him, and he used to say, 'I am Hassan al-Banna's dawah.' He studied under Ibn Baz at the Islamic University and was influenced by Sayyid Qutb, Ibn Taymiyya and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab. He held dawah to be the foundation but argued that entering parliament is obligatory, and was known for dividing tawhid into four parts by adding tawhid of hakimiyya. He refuted the Tijaniyya and Nasser's nationalism. When the sheikh asked why he focused on refuting nationalism and Sufism, he said: because Nasser was the trial of the world. In 2012 he came to Egypt to guide the Salafi sheikhs and urged the Brotherhood to run and take the presidency.
abdulkhaliq.st: A renewer and pioneer; the sheikh heard from him in person.
bk: The Legitimacy of Entering Legislative Councils
Based on the rule 'whatever an obligation depends on is itself obligatory'.
He pushed young people hard to enter parliament to reach application of the Sharia, and failing that to keep what can be kept: if Islam is applied at 50%, don't let it slip to 40%, then 30%.
Refutations of the Tijaniyya and Sufism
Written because Nasser was 'the trial of the world'.
He told the sheikh this directly when asked.

banna: Said: I am Hassan al-Banna's dawah
Al-Banna prayed for him as a child, and his relations with the Brotherhood were good.
ibnbaz: His teacher at the Islamic University
Studied under Ibn Baz in Medina.
hazem: Preferred Sheikh Hazem even while urging the Brotherhood to take the presidency.
huwayni: Al-Huwayni hosted him on al-Hikma channel.
morsi: Went to him with al-Qaradawi to demand a stance on Syria.

hamdawi.s: Founder of Morocco's Islamic Youth; sentenced to death, he emigrated.
hamdawi.l: Sentenced to death, he emigrated to Mecca, then Kuwait for years, then London. The sheikh said he still lives in London, close to 95.

shukrimustafa.s: His group was a violent reaction to torture in prison.
shukrimustafa.l: The sheikh says it had little influence after its time and was not a serious jihadi organisation in the jihadis' own eyes.
shukrimustafa.cr: Extremist; not classified in detail by the sheikh

sirriya.s: Led the 'Military Technical College' cell; not influential.
sirriya.l: Named among the early jihadi organisations of little impact.

sadat.s: Released the Islamists to use them against the Nasserists.
sadat.l: The sheikh says a ruler who wants to finish off his predecessor's camp looks for its enemy, and the Islamic current was the best tool against the left and the Nasserists, so the Brothers were released from 1970 to 1975.

nasser: Wanted to finish off his followers
Used the Islamists against the Nasserists.

ibnbaz.s: 'Salafis in this age never united around a man as they did around him.'
ibnbaz.l: He had spiritual authority over Salafis, even the activists, and harshness towards Islamic groups was not his way. He advised Muhammad al-Ghazali gently and wrote courteous letters to Mawdudi. He interceded for Sayyid Qutb in a letter to Nasser, and was close to Abdullah Azzam. In the Gulf crisis he ruled that seeking American help was permissible out of necessity, on condition the troops left once Saddam was expelled.
ibnbaz.st: The imam of the age for Salafis, gentle with the groups.
ibnbaz.cr: Salafi; the imam of Salafism in his time

qutb: Sent a letter of intercession to Nasser, which stayed sealed until the execution.
ghazali: Despite his mistaken views, advised him kindly.
mawdudi: Despite their disagreements, his letters were full of advice and courtesy.

albani.s: Stood with the Sahwa scholars against seeking non-Muslim help, and said Qutb's words 'have light'.
albani.l: The sheikh notes he sided with Safar al-Hawali and Salman al-Awdah in the Gulf crisis, and quotes him saying some of Qutb's words 'have light'.

qutb: Praised some of Qutb's words in Milestones.
safar: Stood with him in the Gulf crisis

bakrabuzayd.s: Answered Rabee al-Madkhali with a strong letter praising Sayyid Qutb.
bakrabuzayd.l: Rabee al-Madkhali wrote to him attacking Qutb, and he replied with a strong letter setting out Qutb's impact and greatness and rebuking Rabee.

qutb: Set out Qutb's impact and greatness.
rabee: Answered him with a strong letter.

rabee.s: The sheikh sees him as leader of the 'Jamiyya fitna' and attacker of Sayyid Qutb.
rabee.l: According to the sheikh, when the Jamiyya fitna began under his lead he attacked Sayyid Qutb, even saying, 'If I found someone to declare Qutb an unbeliever with me, I would do it', and wrote to Bakr Abu Zayd, who answered him strongly. With the Jami current he aimed his arrows at the Sahwa's leaders.
rabee.st: Sees him as the head of a fitna.
rabee.cr: Jami-Madkhali, which the sheikh calls 'a deviant sect'

qutb: 'If I found someone to declare Qutb an unbeliever with me, I would do it.'
safar: The Jami current aimed at Safar, Salman and Nasser al-Omar.

jami.s: The Jamiyya bears his name; the sheikh says it was 'made and directed' to strike the Sahwa.
jami.l: The sheikh believes the Jami current was created after the Gulf crisis to strike the Sahwa's leaders, and that after 30 years it has no achievements. He says the West recognised the Brotherhood, the jihadis and the Sahwa as enemies but never the Jamiyya.
jami.st: Considers his group a deviant sect.

safar: His current was aimed at the Sahwa
The Jamiyya's war was on those working for Islam.

salman.s: With Safar al-Hawali, one of the Sahwa's two leading figures; the most influential Sunni figure in 2012.
salman.l: He studied under Muhammad Surur in Qassim and carried the banner with Safar al-Hawali, thanks to his scholarly strength and rare intelligence. He rejected seeking non-Muslim help in the Gulf crisis and was imprisoned from 1994 to 1999. In prison he read Muhammad Abduh and 'was somewhat influenced by the rationalist school', although he had written 'A Calm Dialogue with Muhammad al-Ghazali' criticising it. After his release he opened up to non-Salafis, and in 2012 he was named the world's most influential Sunni Islamic figure (first among Islamic figures, fourteenth worldwide). In 2012 he backed Abd al-Mun'im Abu al-Futuh.
salman.st: A major figure, with a reservation about his rationalist influence.
salman.cr: Sahwa Salafi; somewhat influenced by the rationalist school after prison
bk: A Calm Dialogue with Muhammad al-Ghazali
Criticised al-Ghazali's rationalist leanings.
The sheikh notes the irony: he wrote it, then was himself somewhat influenced by the rationalist school after reading Abduh in prison.

surur: Studied under him in the second year of middle school.
ghazali: Answered him in A Calm Dialogue.
tarifi: Al-Tarifi visited him on condition there was no filming.

safar.s: Muhammad Qutb's student and standard-bearer; the first to write on secularism in Arabia.
safar.l: He adopted Muhammad Qutb's view: confront ideas through dawah, without arms and without politics, with change from the base rather than the top; 'this stage may take up the lifetimes of scholars and preachers'. He rejected seeking non-Muslim help in the Gulf crisis and wrote about it. Imprisoned from 1994 to 1999, he later fell ill, stayed home for years and wrote 'Muslims and Western Civilisation'.
safar.st: One of the Sahwa's foremost figures.
bk: Secularism
The first specialised book on secularism in the Arabian Peninsula.
He took the subject from his teacher Muhammad Qutb; the battle over secularism had not yet reached Arabia in force.
Lifting the Gloom from the Scholars of the Nation
Argued the question was not purely legal but about America wanting to stay.
Written in the Gulf crisis: America wanted to come and occupy the region, 'the first time infidel armies came to the land of Muhammad ﷺ and settled there'.
Kissinger's Promise
On America's ambitions in the Peninsula.
Mentioned with Lifting the Gloom in the Gulf crisis context.
Muslims and Western Civilisation
Written during his illness; includes his advice to scholars.

The sheikh quotes its story of a foreign soldier: 'Japan made a mouse that eats mice... how the king needs a religious mouse to eat the religious', and Safar's comment: the Arabs said 'every thing has a pest of its own kind'.

ibnbaz: Differed with his fatwa on seeking help
Held seeking non-Muslim help impermissible while Ibn Baz allowed it out of necessity.

nasseromar.s: A Sahwa figure jailed from 1994 to 1999, focused on spiritual formation.
nasseromar.l: Named among the Sahwa leaders targeted by the Jami current and jailed in 1994, and as an advocate of tarbiya.

azzam.s: A Palestinian Brother who moved to Afghanistan, where the jihadi current took shape.
azzam.l: Originally from the Brotherhood in Palestine, he moved to Afghanistan when jihad against the Soviets opened in 1979 with government backing. He was close to Ibn Baz. The sheikh says the Brotherhood, especially its international body, gave him little support, which grieved him. He was assassinated at the end of 1989.

hudaybi: The international organisation gave him little support.

ahmedyassin.s: Founder of Hamas, the Brotherhood's jihad exception.
ahmedyassin.l: Mentioned with prayers of mercy; the sheikh holds that everyone agrees on supporting the mujahideen in Palestine.

khomeini.s: His revolution and its export were among the providential causes of the Sahwa.
khomeini.l: The sheikh says the Iranian revolution and Shi'ism had to be met with a counter-idea, which was Islam and especially Salafism, so the Sahwa grew stronger.

juhayman.s: His incident on 1/1/1400 AH was a providential cause of the Sahwa.
juhayman.l: The sheikh mentions his incident as a providential cause of the Sahwa's growth, noting that when a jihadi current is crushed, room opens for dawah-based Islam.
juhayman.st: Mentioned as an event, not a model.

zia.s: His assassination is mentioned among the events that closed the door of jihad.
zia.l: Mentioned with Azzam's assassination and the closing of jihad at the end of the 1980s.

saddam.s: His invasion of Kuwait divided the groups and led to the rise of the Jamiyya.
saddam.l: After he invaded Kuwait the Brotherhood split into supporters, opponents and the silent; all Salafis rejected it, but they split over seeking non-Muslim help.

mawdudi.l: He coined the term hakimiyya, yet did not take it to mean avoiding politics; his party entered politics and he was sentenced to death several times. His books, with Qutb's, were core literature, and his name angered Hebrew University lecturers. Despite his disagreement with Ibn Baz, Ibn Baz wrote to him courteously.
mawdudi.st: One of the names that most worried the West.

ibnbaz: Ibn Baz sent him letters of advice and courtesy.

nadwi.s: Author of 'What the World Lost by the Decline of Muslims'.
nadwi.l: The sheikh says his book spread because the Brotherhood adopted it, so with Qutb and Mawdudi it formed literature that shielded Muslims from Western influence.
bk: What the World Lost by the Decline of Muslims
Spread widely because the Brotherhood adopted it.
One of the 'shields' against Western influence in the Islamic current.

erbakan.s: Took politics alone as the path to reform in Turkey.
erbakan.l: The sheikh puts him in the fourth category of approaches: politics only.

erdogan.s: 'Are you not content that I be your Negus... and later your Joseph?'
erdogan.l: As mayor of Istanbul and then prime minister, when Turkey's Salafis asked him to apply the Sharia, he said: 'Are you not content that I be your Negus?', meaning he would protect them, and they accepted. As president he said: 'Are you not content that I be your Joseph?', meaning he would open space for dawah. The sheikh says America let him rise, then 'discovered it was a trick and regretted it'.
erdogan.st: The model of the Negus, then of Joseph, not of the Prophet ﷺ.

erbakan: His party followed Erbakan with the same approach.

turabi.s: Founded his movement in Sudan, drawing in Brotherhood defectors.
turabi.l: Named among the causes of the multiplication of groups after the Brotherhood's absence.

ghannouchi.s: A hunted exile who despaired of change in Tunisia, then was in power months later.
ghannouchi.l: The sheikh cites him to show that no one can predict great changes, and says his party's positions are 'barely distinguishable from secularism'.

kishk.s: 'Knight of the pulpits' and 'king of the cassettes', a man of rare courage.
kishk.l: The sheikh says he had the greatest impact in the Muslim world in the 1970s and 80s, and that through his tapes and sermons God brought down much of the falsehood Nasser had built.

nasser: His tapes brought down much of what Nasser had built.

qattan.s: An influential Sahwa preacher who told the sheikh why he stopped preaching.
qattan.l: He was very influential until he was removed from preaching. The sheikh asked him why he stopped and left the scene, and he said it was at Obama's request and order. (This is al-Qattan's account as the sheikh reports it.)
qattan.st: One of the most influential preachers.

qahtani.s: A highly influential preacher; Muhammad al-Arifi turned to religion through him.
qahtani.l: He rose before the 1990s with great impact, and 'the most famous preacher of the recent era', Muhammad al-Arifi, became religious through him.

arifi: Al-Arifi turned to religion through him

arifi.s: 'The first and most influential preacher in the Arab world' at the start of the millennium.
arifi.l: He was number one on Twitter in a 2012 ranking (eight of the top ten were preachers). His PhD, on Ibn Taymiyya's stance on Sufism, earned excellent with honours. He backed al-Tarifi when his account was hacked, spreading his reach. The sheikh began his own journey with al-Arifi's first recorded tape.
arifi.st: A preacher who was also a solid student of knowledge.
bk: Ibn Taymiyya's Stance on Sufism
Awarded excellent with honours.
The sheikh uses it to show the preachers of that era were solid students of knowledge, not 'devoid of knowledge'.
The End of the World
Its hadiths were verified and graded by Sheikh al-Tarifi.
The start of the relationship between al-Arifi and al-Tarifi.

tarifi: When al-Tarifi's account was hacked, al-Arifi backed him and his reach grew enormously.
qahtani: Sa'id ibn Misfir was the cause of his guidance.

awadi.s: One of the leading preachers of the late 1990s, with a PhD in mathematics.
awadi.l: Very bright: top of his class with 100% in high school, outstanding at university, a doctor of mathematics who teaches it. He was among the most influential on Twitter in 2012.

abdulmuhsin.s: One of the preachers who rose in the late 1990s.
abdulmuhsin.l: Named after Nabil al-Awadi among that era's preachers.

khalidrashid.s: 'The strongest influence on people's hearts', known for the lecture 'O Nation of Muhammad'.
khalidrashid.l: The sheikh says he 'planted faith deep in people's hearts', in nine years of work in all. Ordinary young people handed out his tapes and many became religious because of him, so much so that youths in other Arab countries told the sheikh, 'We know him better than you do.'
khalidrashid.st: The preacher with the strongest effect on hearts.
bk: O Nation of Muhammad
'The most widely spread lecture since Islamists began making tapes.'
In defence of the Prophet ﷺ. The sheikh says: 'I don't recall hearing a stronger lecture to this day', and that his stand in it was stronger than all the scholars' combined.
Caravans of the Returning
Very effective in leading youth to religion.
Young people handed them out at the start of the 2000s.

shugairi.s: Among the most influential on Twitter in 2012.
shugairi.l: Named on the 2012 list of Twitter's most influential.

tarifi.s: 'The model of the complete scholar who fights Islam's battle'; the current's strongest pillar 2008–2016.
tarifi.l: Launched by al-Majd channel at about 32 with a Ramadan programme. His account was hacked at 85,000 followers and al-Arifi backed him. The Sahwa adopted him as a leader in a broad current with no central leadership, and after his famous fatwa on detainees the jihadi current leaned towards him too, so he influenced both wings. In 2012 he travelled to Egypt and urged people on al-Hikma channel to vote for Hazem Salah Abu Ismail. He was imprisoned in 2016.
tarifi.st: The foremost scholar of his period.
bk: Fatwa on the detainees
Through it the jihadi current leaned towards him.
It made him influential in both the Sahwa and jihadi currents; people waited for his fatwas.

arifi: Repaid al-Arifi's support by praising him on al-Risala channel.
hazem: Urged people to vote for him
Said on al-Hikma: I call on you to vote for Sheikh Hazem.
salman: Visited him on condition of no filming

huwayni.s: The most influential figure for students and youth in Egypt; he 'ignited a love of hadith'.
huwayni.l: He led Egypt's Salafi current before the Arab Spring, and many youths turned to hadith studies because of his lectures. He welcomed Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq at the airport and hosted him. In 2012 he said: 'I say to the whole world: vote for Sheikh Hazem.'

hazem: Urged people to vote for him
abdulkhaliq: Held lectures with him on al-Hikma channel.

muhammadhassan.s: Influential among the general public more than among students.
muhammadhassan.l: The sheikh says his influence was broad, not on students or youth as al-Huwayni's was.

yaqub.s: An Egyptian Salafi sheikh focused on spiritual formation.
yaqub.l: Named among Egypt's sheikhs concerned with tarbiya.

abdulmaqsud.s: 'Among the first to go down with the people' in the Egyptian revolution.
abdulmaqsud.l: One of Cairo's Salafis, known for great courage, and among the first to join the people in the revolution and remind them.

fawzi.s: One of Cairo's Salafis, known for great courage.
fawzi.l: Named with Muhammad Abd al-Maqsud and Nashat Ahmad.

nashat.s: Tortured to make him attack al-Huwayni, he refused: 'We did not betray and we will not.'
nashat.l: He relates that he was tortured in prison, his bones broken and given electric shocks until his body turned black, to make him speak against al-Huwayni, and he refused. The sheikh sees this as 'the way of the criminals in toppling scholars': torturing one sheikh to make him attack an influential one. The sheikh says he lives in exile in Denmark or Sweden.

huwayni: Refused to attack him under torture
'We did not betray and we will not.'

muqaddim.s: An Alexandrian Salafi with a good impact.
muqaddim.l: Named as the symbol of Alexandria Salafism.

hazem.s: 'The most outstanding man of modern times in awareness'; the man of complete solutions.
hazem.l: The sheikh sees him as 'the only one who was aware' during the Arab Spring, a man of piercing insight. His father was in the Brotherhood, and he was close to the Salafi sheikhs and al-Huwayni. He relied heavily on Sayyid Qutb. He ran for president in 2012 with the backing of most sheikhs, even those who reject politics, and won his debates, even winning some Christian support. He was disqualified over the claim his mother was American, and founded al-Raya Party. He knew his 'historical role' and saw his position like Joseph's: 'Set me over the storehouses of the land.' He criticised Morsi: 'You are spending our popular credit.'
hazem.st: A rare man; he was in the right.

morsi: Criticised him without handing the enemy an opening
'Mr President, you are now spending our popular credit.'
huwayni: Al-Huwayni led the scene before the Arab Spring.
qutb: Developed Qutb's ideas and gathered evidence for them.

rifaisurur.s: A jihadi-current sheikh who urged a vote for Hazem 'as a phenomenon for applying the Sharia'.
rifaisurur.l: He said: 'I vote for Hazem as a phenomenon for applying the Sharia.'

hazem: Urged people to vote for him
Backed him as a phenomenon for applying the Sharia.

abufutuh.s: The 2012 candidate of the 'general' current that favours humanist language.
abufutuh.l: Salman al-Awdah, al-Qaradawi and a group from the current that prefers general language leaned towards him.

qaradawi.s: Left the Brotherhood and backed Abu al-Futuh 'forever and ever'.
qaradawi.l: The sheikh says he 'is not counted with the Brotherhood as a group'; he did not back Khairat al-Shater but said, 'I am with Abd al-Mun'im Abu al-Futuh forever and ever.' He went with Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq to Morsi to demand a stance on Syria.

morsi: Demanded a clear stance from him.

shater.s: The Brotherhood's first 2012 candidate before his disqualification.
shater.l: The plan was for him to rule if elected; he was disqualified and Muhammad Morsi came as the substitute.

morsi.s: Reached power 'by a narrow margin' and could not run the country.
morsi.l: The sheikh believes the battle was beyond the Brotherhood's capacity, and that blaming the enemies' scheming is 'an invalid excuse'. After Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq and al-Qaradawi pressed him, he declared at a stadium rally, 'There is no place for Hezbollah in Syria', and, according to the sheikh, America then hastened his fall.
morsi.st: We pray for mercy on him and pardon those who erred.

shafik: The battle was between the Islamists led by the Brotherhood and Islam's enemies led by Shafik.

shafik.s: The 'deep state' candidate, backed by the Jamiyya and the Sufis.
shafik.l: The sheikh says the Jamiyya, the Sufis and the secularists backed him in 2012.
shafik.st: Led Islam's enemies in the election.

hamidali.s: A Kuwaiti Sahwa preacher who filled the gap after the scholars were jailed.
hamidali.l: Named with Hakim al-Mutairi and Abd al-Razzaq al-Shayji.

hakim.s: One of the names that rose in the late 1990s 'and is still prominent'.
hakim.l: Named among the new reform figures the Islamic current produced.

shayji.s: A Kuwaiti Sahwa preacher of the late 1990s.
shayji.l: Named with Hamid al-Ali and Hakim al-Mutairi.

abumusab.s: 'A theorist of the jihadi current'; the sheikh quotes him that takfir began spontaneously, then became organised.
abumusab.l: Cited to describe how takfir spread among the currents in the 1990s.

ahmadsayyid.s: One of the people behind the 'Sina'at al-Muhawir' programme, which preserved many young people's faith.
ahmadsayyid.l: The sheikh says the programme played a great historical role for about four years in preserving people's faith after the Arab Spring, when atheism and doubts spread.
bk: Sina'at al-Muhawir (Making the Debater)
Preserved many young Muslims at a critical time.
It came when atheism had become a phenomenon even among the children of sheikhs and preachers, and when people like Shahrour and Adnan Ibrahim dominated Ramadan TV talk about Islam.

ujayri: They worked together on Sina'at al-Muhawir.
ameri: They worked together on Sina'at al-Muhawir.
shahrour: The programme confronted the wave of doubts.

ujayri.s: One of the people behind Sina'at al-Muhawir.
ujayri.l: Named with Ahmad al-Sayyid and Sami Ameri.

ahmadsayyid: Worked with him on the programme.

ameri.s: One of the people behind Sina'at al-Muhawir.
ameri.l: Named with Ahmad al-Sayyid and Abdullah al-Ujayri.

ahmadsayyid: Worked with him on the programme.

shahrour.s: One of those who 'lead people away from their religion' on Ramadan programmes.
shahrour.l: Mentioned in the wave of doubts after the Arab Spring.

adnanibrahim.s: 'Led people astray', as the sheikh puts it.
adnanibrahim.l: Mentioned with Shahrour in the wave of doubts.

sakran.s: Joined the Islamic current providentially, not through anyone's dawah; his books 'strengthened many young people'.
sakran.l: The sheikh prays for his release and steadfastness. He tells al-Sakran's childhood story of stadium youths moving to the mosques, and says his books are important 'but not enough'; the Qur'an must be central.

faridansari.s: His books are important 'but not enough' compared with living with the Qur'an itself.
faridansari.l: Mentioned in the final episode: many youths read books of spiritual purification like Farid al-Ansari's; they are important but cannot replace entering the Qur'an 'as one seeking guidance'.

raedsalah.s: Related how Hebrew University lecturers got angry when 'Milestones' was mentioned.
raedsalah.l: The sheikh uses his account to show how much the names Qutb and Mawdudi worried the West.

abdulsalamarif.s: Intervened with Nasser to soften Qutb's death sentence.
abdulsalamarif.l: Named among the Arab rulers who tried to mediate.

qutb: Tried to soften the death sentence.

alitantawi.s: In his memoirs, told the beard story from a time when religious practice was not visible.
alitantawi.l: Asked about the beard, he said it was obligatory, 'but I cannot bear to go against people', then God helped him and he grew it. The sheikh uses it to show conditions before the Sahwa.

ghadban.s: Author of 'The Activist Method of the Prophet's Biography', drawing on Qutb.
ghadban.l: Counted among those influenced by Qutb's opening of the activist method.
bk: The Activist Method of the Prophet's Biography
Written drawing on 'In the Shade of the Qur'an'.
An example of Qutb's reach into biographies of the Prophet.

salahkhalidi.s: 'Knows Sayyid better than his brother Muhammad Qutb'; Qutb's biographer.
salahkhalidi.l: The sheikh refers anyone wanting the details of Sayyid Qutb's life to him.
bk: Sayyid Qutb from Birth to Martyrdom
The fullest biography of Qutb.
Muhammad Qutb told those who asked about his brother: ask Salah Abd al-Fattah, he knows Sayyid better than I do.

rashadsalim.s: Edited and published Ibn Taymiyya's major works.
rashadsalim.l: The sheikh says Ibn Taymiyya's books did not spread widely until he edited and published them.

bennabi.s: Sayyid Qutb answered him in 'Milestones' on the meaning of civilisation.
bennabi.l: Qutb used to write 'the civilised Islamic society', then dropped 'civilised', saying an Islamic society is by definition civilised, and answered Malik Bennabi on this.

binibrahim.s: 'A partner in authority', so Arabia had no need for groups.
binibrahim.l: The sheikh uses him to explain why activist groups were absent from Arabia: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab's dawah was dominant, and Sheikh Muhammad ibn Ibrahim influenced decision-making.

sacidhawwa.s: One of the thinkers whose books the Brotherhood banned in the 1980s.
sacidhawwa.l: Mentioned as evidence of the Brotherhood stifling its own cadres.

tawfiqshawi.s: 'Don't read him': one of the thinkers whose books the Brotherhood banned.
tawfiqshawi.l: Named with Sa'id Hawwa and al-Nafisi.

ahmedmansour.s: Host of 'Witness to the Era', a source for the history of the groups.
ahmedmansour.l: The sheikh counts him among TV sources for the groups' history, but 'it doesn't give you the full picture'.

azzamtamimi.s: Interviewed leaders of the groups; a source for their history.
azzamtamimi.l: Mentioned with Ahmed Mansour as a partial source.

bush.s: Declared it a 'crusade': 'you are either with us or against us'.
bush.l: The sheikh says America used September 11 as a pretext to invade Afghanistan, then invaded Iraq in 2003 'and empowered the Rafida there'.

macron.s: Mentioned over the insults to the Prophet ﷺ and the boycott of France.
macron.l: The sheikh notes some Jami figures opposed the boycott, and holds that the nation's causes allow no neutrality: 'either with the Prophet ﷺ or with Macron'.
macron.st: An adversary on the question of the Prophet ﷺ.
